title: The Name Hidden in God's Promise to Hagar
paragraphs:
The Name Hidden in God's Promise to Hagar
The God Who Sees the Forgotten, Hears the Broken, and Rewrites Every Scandal into Grace

There are stories in Scripture that many believers quietly pass over. They are uncomfortable. They are messy. They involve broken homes, jealousy, abuse, desperation, and consequences that seem impossible to untangle. Yet hidden inside one of those painful stories is one of the most breathtaking revelations of God's character in the entire Bible.
It is not found in a palace.
It is not spoken to a king.
It is not first revealed to Abraham.
It is revealed to a rejected slave woman crying alone in the wilderness.
Her name was Hagar.
And through her tears, God revealed a Name that still comforts every forgotten soul today.
Perhaps that is where you are right now.
Not physically in a desert...
But emotionally.
Spiritually.
Quietly wondering if God still notices you after all the mistakes, all the rejection, all the disappointments, and all the people who have walked away.
If so, this story was preserved in Scripture for you.
Because before God became known as the Deliverer of Israel...
Before He revealed Himself at Sinai...
Before David sang about Him...
Before Isaiah prophesied about the Messiah...
A broken woman looked into heaven through her tears and gave God a Name that has echoed through history.
Not because she understood everything.
But because she discovered something unforgettable.
God sees.
When Human Plans Replace God's Promise
The account begins in Genesis 16.
God had promised Abram and Sarai that they would have descendants as numerous as the stars (Genesis 15).
Yet years passed.
Nothing happened.
Waiting became frustration.
Frustration became fear.
Fear became human planning.
Sarai offered her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram so they could obtain the promised heir through cultural customs common in the ancient Near East.

Although culturally accepted, Scripture never presents this as God's design for marriage or covenant faithfulness. Instead, Genesis simply records what happened without approving it. Throughout the Bible, narratives often describe human actions honestly while allowing the consequences to reveal God's wisdom.
The Hebrew repeatedly highlights the tragic progression. In Genesis 16:2, Sarai says:

וַיֹּאמֶר שָׂרַי אֶל־אַבְרָם... בֹּא־נָא אֶל־שִׁפְחָתִי
"Come now to my servant..."
The language intentionally echoes humanity's recurring temptation to secure God's promises through human effort rather than trusting His timing.
What followed was predictable.
Pregnancy.
Jealousy.
Conflict.
Bitterness.
Abuse.
Eventually Hagar fled into the wilderness.
Not because she lacked faith.
Because she had nowhere left to go.
Sometimes people run because they are rebellious.
Sometimes people run because they are wounded.
Scripture tells us Hagar fled after Sarai dealt harshly with her (Genesis 16:6).

The Hebrew verb is עָנָה (ʿānâ), a word that can describe affliction, oppression, or being humbled through suffering. It is the same family of language later used to describe Israel's oppression in Egypt. The Bible does not minimize Hagar's pain. God sees it clearly.
The Angel of the LORD Appears
Then something astonishing happens.
Genesis 16:7 says:
"The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness."
Notice carefully.
Hagar did not find God.
God found Hagar.
Grace almost always moves first.
The Hebrew says:

וַיִּמְצָאָהּ מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה
Vayyimtza'ehā mal'akh YHWH.
Literally:
"The Messenger of Yahweh found her."

Throughout the Old Testament, "the Angel of the LORD" often speaks with divine authority, receives worship, forgives sins, and identifies Himself as God. Many Christian scholars understand several of these appearances as a pre-incarnate manifestation of Christ—the eternal Son revealing Himself before His incarnation. While faithful interpreters have discussed these passages in different ways, this view fits the text's remarkable portrayal of the Messenger speaking as God Himself.
Long before Bethlehem...
Long before the manger...
Long before the cross...
The Lord was already seeking the broken.
"You Shall Call His Name Ishmael"
Then God gives Hagar a promise.
Genesis 16:11:

וְקָרָאת שְׁמוֹ יִשְׁמָעֵאל
Veqārā't shemô Yishmaʿel.
"You shall call his name Ishmael."
The Hebrew name יִשְׁמָעֵאל (Yishmaʿel) comes from two elements:
שָׁמַע (shāmaʿ) — "to hear"
and
אֵל (El) — "God."
His name literally means:
"God hears."
The angel explains why:
כִּי־שָׁמַע יְהוָה אֶל־עָנְיֵךְ
"Because the LORD has heard your affliction."
Not because Hagar was famous.
Not because she was powerful.
Not because she belonged to Israel.
God heard her because she cried.
This anticipates a consistent biblical theme: the Lord hears the oppressed, the repentant, and those who call upon Him in faith (Psalm 34:17; Exodus 3:7; Romans 10:13).
The Name Hidden in the Wilderness
Then comes one of the greatest moments in all of Genesis.
Genesis 16:13 says:
"So she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, 'You are a God of seeing,' for she said, 'Truly here I have seen Him who looks after me.'"
The Hebrew reads:

אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי
Attah El Ro'i.
Usually translated:
"You are the God who sees me."
This title is often written as El Roi.
The Hebrew root is:
רָאָה (ra'ah)
meaning:
to see
to perceive
to notice
to pay attention
to look with understanding.
This is far more than visual observation.
God was not merely looking at Hagar.
He understood her.
Every tear.
Every fear.
Every unanswered question.
Every lonely mile through the desert.
Every silent cry.
Every hidden wound.
God saw everything.
How many people today desperately want someone to truly see them?
Social media shows followers.
God sees hearts.
Crowds notice success.
God notices suffering.
People measure appearance.
God measures truth.
Many feel invisible in their own homes, churches, workplaces, or families.
But Hagar's story declares that no child of God is invisible to Him.
Jesus Becomes the Ultimate Fulfillment
The Gospel reveals this same divine compassion in Jesus Christ.
When Jesus met the Samaritan woman in John 4, He knew her entire past and still offered her living water.
When He called Zacchaeus down from the tree, He saw the man beneath the reputation.
When He stopped for blind Bartimaeus, He heard the voice others tried to silence.
When He looked at Peter after the denial, His gaze carried conviction and mercy.
When Mary Magdalene wept outside the empty tomb, the risen Christ spoke her name.
The same God who saw Hagar became flesh.
John 1:14 declares:

Καὶ ὁ Λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
"Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto."
"And the Word became flesh."
Jesus did not come merely to observe humanity.
He entered our suffering.
He bore our sin.
He carried our shame.
Isaiah 53:4 says:
"He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows."
The cross proves forever that God's gaze is never detached. In Christ, God entered our brokenness to redeem it.
The story of Hagar begins with scandal.
Broken relationships.
Human failure.
Poor decisions.
Pain.
Abandonment.
Yet that is not where God leaves the story.
That pattern unfolds throughout Scripture.
Rahab moved from prostitution to becoming part of the Messianic line.
Ruth moved from widowhood to redemption.
David moved from adultery and repentance to restored fellowship.
Peter moved from denial to bold proclamation.
Paul moved from persecutor to apostle.
And all of us who trust in Christ move from sinners under condemnation to redeemed children of God, not because of our merit but because of His grace (Ephesians 2:8–9).
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not that sin is ignored.
Not that consequences disappear.
But that through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, grace has the final word.
That is why our theme remains:
The God Who Still Sees You
Perhaps you are carrying secrets no one else knows.
Perhaps you smile in public while silently grieving.
Perhaps your prayers feel unanswered.
Perhaps you think your failures have disqualified you.
Remember Hagar.
The first person in Scripture to give God a descriptive name was not an influential leader but a hurting servant in the wilderness.
That alone reminds us that God's grace reaches far beyond human expectations.
If He saw Hagar...
He sees you.
If He heard Hagar...
He hears you.
If He met Hagar in the wilderness...
He can meet you wherever you are.
But the greatest invitation is not simply to know that God sees you.
It is to respond to the One who came to save you.

Jesus Christ lived the sinless life we could never live, died for our sins, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Everyone who repents and believes in Him receives forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and the gift of eternal life (Acts 3:19; John 3:16; Romans 10:9–10).
Grace is not permission to remain in sin.
Grace is God's power to leave it behind and walk in newness of life.

If this story reminded you that God still sees the forgotten and rewrites lives through Jesus Christ, don't let it end here. Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else has been praying for.
Your support enables us to continue producing carefully researched articles, devotionals, discipleship resources, and Gospel-centered content that points people to Jesus Christ.
One soul reached with the Gospel is worth more than a lifetime spent chasing applause.
